notes:
1. Written Constitution

  • The Constitution of India is a written Constitution.
  • Its fundamental rules are contained in an authoritative constitutional document.
  • It expressly defines the structure, powers and functions of important governmental institutions.
  • It contains provisions relating to the Union, States, Judiciary, rights, elections, public services, emergencies and constitutional bodies.
  • Constitutional amendments become part of this written constitutional framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Written Constitution

2. Detailed and Comprehensive Constitution

  • The Indian Constitution is one of the world's most detailed written constitutions.

The original Constitution contained:

  • 395 Articles.
  • 22 Parts.
  • 8 Schedules.
  • It presently contains 12 Schedules.

Its detailed nature reflects India's:

  • Large territory.
  • Population.
  • Social diversity.
  • Linguistic diversity.
  • Federal arrangements.
  • Administrative complexity.
  • Many matters left to conventions in some countries are expressly regulated in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Original Constitution → 395 Articles + 22 Parts + 8 Schedules

3. Constitution Drawn from Various Sources

  • The Constitution-makers studied several foreign constitutional systems.
  • They did not mechanically copy foreign provisions.
  • Suitable provisions were modified and adapted to Indian conditions.
  • The Government of India Act, 1935 supplied a large part of the administrative framework.
  • The national movement, Indian political experience and Constituent Assembly debates also shaped the Constitution.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Constitution → Borrowed Features + Indian Adaptation

4. Important Foreign Constitutional Influences

  • United Kingdom influenced parliamentary government, Cabinet responsibility, Rule of Law and single citizenship.
  • United States influenced Fundamental Rights, judicial review and independence of the Judiciary.
  • Ireland influenced the Directive Principles of State Policy.
  • Canada influenced federation with a strong Centre and Union residuary powers.
  • Australia influenced the Concurrent List and joint sitting.
  • Former Soviet Union influenced Fundamental Duties.
  • France influenced Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
  • Germany influenced emergency-related provisions.
  • South Africa influenced constitutional amendment procedure.
  • Japan influenced the expression "procedure established by law."
📌 Must-Memorise

UK → Parliamentary System

USA → Fundamental Rights

Ireland → DPSP

Canada → Strong Centre

Australia → Concurrent List

USSR → Duties

Germany → Emergency

South Africa → Amendment

Japan → Procedure Established by Law

5. Sovereign Constitutional Order

  • India is a sovereign State.
  • Indian governmental authority is not constitutionally subordinate to any external political authority.
  • India exercises independent authority over its internal and external affairs.
  • All governmental institutions within India derive their authority from the Constitution.

6. Democratic System

  • India follows representative democracy.
  • Citizens elect representatives through periodic elections.
  • Governments are accountable through democratic institutions.
  • Universal adult franchise gives eligible adult citizens the right to vote.
  • Political power can change peacefully through elections.
  • Democracy operates at the Union, State and local levels.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Representative Democracy

7. Republic

  • India is a republic.
  • The head of State is not a hereditary monarch.
  • The President of India is the constitutional head of the Union.
  • The office of President is elective.
  • Republic therefore refers primarily to the non-hereditary nature of the headship of State.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Republic → Elected/Non-Hereditary Head of State

It does not mean that the President must be directly elected by the people.

8. Parliamentary Form of Government

  • India follows the parliamentary form of government.
  • The parliamentary system operates at both Union and State levels.
  • The President is the constitutional or nominal executive at the Union level.
  • The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers constitute the real political executive.
  • The Governor is the constitutional head at the State level.
  • The Chief Minister and Council of Ministers constitute the real political executive in the State.
  • The Executive remains politically accountable to the Legislature.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union → President = Constitutional Head

Prime Minister = Real Political Executive

State → Governor = Constitutional Head

Chief Minister = Real Political Executive

9. Collective Responsibility

  • Collective responsibility is a central feature of parliamentary government.
  • Article 75(3) provides that the Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
  • At the State level, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
  • Ministers function as a team.
  • A ministry that loses the confidence of the Lower House cannot normally continue in office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union Council of Ministers → Collectively Responsible to Lok Sabha

10. Fusion of Executive and Legislature

  • India does not maintain a complete institutional separation between the Legislature and political Executive.
  • Ministers are generally members of the Legislature.
  • A person appointed as minister who is not a member of Parliament must become a member within the constitutionally prescribed period.
  • The Executive therefore emerges from and remains accountable to the Legislature.
  • This is different from the presidential system, where the Executive and Legislature are more strictly separated.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

India → Parliamentary System

USA → Presidential System

11. Nominal and Real Executive

  • The Constitution creates a distinction between the formal head and the real political executive.
  • The President performs constitutional functions generally on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
  • The Governor performs a corresponding constitutional role at the State level, subject to constitutional provisions.
  • Actual day-to-day political leadership lies with the Prime Minister and Chief Ministers.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Parliamentary Government → Nominal Executive + Real Executive

12. Federal Constitutional Structure

  • India has a federal distribution of governmental powers.
  • Government operates at the Union and State levels.
  • Both Union and State governments derive authority from the Constitution.
  • Legislative powers are constitutionally distributed.
  • The Constitution is supreme over both levels.
  • Courts resolve constitutional disputes between governments.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Federal Constitutional Structure

13. Major Federal Features

Important federal characteristics include:

  • Dual polity consisting of Union and States.
  • Written Constitution.
  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Division of legislative powers.
  • Partly rigid constitutional amendment procedure.
  • Independent judiciary.
  • Bicameral Parliament.
  • Representation of States in the Rajya Sabha.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Federalism → Constitutional Division of Powers

14. Seventh Schedule and Distribution of Powers

The Seventh Schedule contains three legislative lists:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.
  • Parliament ordinarily legislates on Union List matters.
  • State Legislatures ordinarily legislate on State List matters.
  • Both Parliament and State Legislatures may legislate on Concurrent List subjects, subject to constitutional rules.
  • This distribution forms a central feature of Indian federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seventh Schedule → Union + State + Concurrent Lists

15. Federation with a Strong Centre

  • Indian federalism gives the Union comparatively strong constitutional powers.
  • Residuary legislative powers belong to Parliament.
  • Parliament possesses important powers during emergencies.
  • Parliament can alter the area, boundaries and names of States according to constitutional procedure.
  • Governors are appointed by the President.
  • All India Services connect Union and State administration.
  • The integrated judicial system also strengthens constitutional unity.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Federal System with Strong Central Features

16. Article 1 — Union of States

  • Article 1 declares: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."
  • The Constitution uses the expression "Union of States."
  • It does not describe India in Article 1 as a "Federation of States."
  • States do not possess a constitutional right to secede from India.
  • The expression emphasises the indestructible constitutional unity of the Indian Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1 → India, that is Bharat → Union of States

17. Parliament's Power over State Territory

  • Parliament may form new States.
  • It may increase or diminish the area of a State.
  • It may alter State boundaries.
  • It may alter the name of a State.
  • These powers operate through Articles 2, 3 and related constitutional provisions.
  • A State Legislature can express its views when constitutionally required, but its consent is not an absolute constitutional requirement for Parliament to reorganise States.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Union → Indestructible Union with Alterable State Boundaries

18. Unitary or Centralising Features

Important centralising features include:

  • Strong Union government.
  • Residuary powers with Parliament.
  • Single citizenship.
  • Integrated judiciary.
  • Appointment of Governors by the President.
  • All India Services.
  • Emergency provisions.
  • Parliament's power over State reorganisation.
  • Integrated constitutional institutions such as the Election Commission and CAG.
  • Union authority over specified matters during exceptional circumstances.

19. Quasi-Federal Character

  • K.C. Wheare famously described the Indian Constitution as "quasi-federal."
  • The expression refers to a federal structure containing strong centralising characteristics.
  • "Quasi-federal" is a scholarly description.
  • It is not an expression used by the Constitution itself.
  • Other scholars have emphasised the cooperative nature of Indian federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

K.C. Wheare → Quasi-Federal

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

"Quasi-Federal" → Scholarly Description

Not Constitutional Terminology

20. Cooperative Federalism

  • The Union and States do not function in complete isolation.
  • Many governmental programmes require cooperation between both levels.
  • Financial relations require regular Union–State interaction.
  • Institutions such as the Finance Commission assist fiscal coordination.
  • The Inter-State Council provides a constitutional mechanism for intergovernmental consultation.
  • Cooperative federalism therefore operates alongside the constitutional division of powers.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Federalism → Division of Powers + Cooperation

21. Asymmetrical Federalism

  • The Constitution does not apply an identical institutional arrangement to every territory.
  • Some States and regions possess special constitutional provisions.
  • Articles 371 to 371J contain special provisions relating to specified States.
  • Scheduled and tribal areas receive special constitutional protection.
  • Union Territories are governed through arrangements different from ordinary States.
  • This unequal but constitutionally designed distribution of arrangements is commonly described as asymmetrical federalism.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Federalism → Not Completely Symmetrical

22. Blend of Rigidity and Flexibility

  • The Constitution is neither completely rigid nor completely flexible.
  • Certain constitutional matters may be changed through a simple parliamentary majority.
  • Most amendments require a special majority.

Specified federal provisions require:

  • Special majority in Parliament.
  • Ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures.
  • The amendment procedure therefore combines stability with adaptability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Constitution → Partly Rigid + Partly Flexible

23. Article 368 and Amendment

  • Article 368 deals with Parliament's constituent power and procedure for constitutional amendment.
  • Most constitutional amendments require a special parliamentary majority.
  • Certain federal amendments require State ratification.
  • There is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve disagreement between the Houses on a Constitution Amendment Bill.
  • Constitutional amendment therefore differs from ordinary law-making.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 368 → Constitutional Amendment

24. Constitutional Supremacy

  • The Constitution is the supreme law of India.
  • Parliament must legislate within constitutional limits.
  • State Legislatures must also act within constitutionally assigned powers.
  • The Executive is bound by constitutional and legal limitations.
  • Courts may examine laws and governmental actions for constitutional validity.
  • India therefore does not follow unlimited parliamentary sovereignty.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Constitutional Supremacy

25. Parliamentary Power and Judicial Review

  • The Indian constitutional system combines substantial parliamentary power with judicial review.
  • Parliament possesses broad legislative authority.
  • Parliament also possesses constitutional-amending power.
  • Courts may invalidate laws that violate constitutional limitations.
  • Constitutional amendments themselves are subject to the Basic Structure limitation.
  • India therefore combines aspects of parliamentary government with strong constitutional judicial safeguards.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

India → Parliamentary Government + Judicial Review

26. Independent Judiciary

  • Judicial independence is a major constitutional feature.
  • Judges are expected to decide cases without political interference.
  • Supreme Court and High Court judges receive constitutional protection concerning tenure and removal.
  • Their service conditions are constitutionally protected.
  • Judicial independence helps protect the Constitution, rights and federal balance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Independent Judiciary → Guardian of Constitution

27. Integrated Judicial System

  • India has a single integrated judicial system.
  • The Supreme Court stands at the apex.
  • High Courts function below the Supreme Court within the constitutional hierarchy.
  • Subordinate courts function under the supervision of High Courts.
  • India does not maintain entirely separate federal and State judicial systems like some classical federations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Supreme Court → High Courts → Subordinate Courts

28. Judicial Review

  • Judicial review permits courts to examine the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions.
  • Article 13 is important in relation to laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
  • Article 32 gives the Supreme Court power to enforce Fundamental Rights.
  • Article 226 gives High Courts extensive writ jurisdiction.
  • Judicial review helps maintain constitutional supremacy.
  • Judicial review has also been recognised as part of the Basic Structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Judicial Review → Constitutional Supremacy

Article 32 → Supreme Court

Article 226 → High Courts

29. Basic Structure Doctrine

  • Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368.
  • In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973, the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
  • Basic Structure elements have been developed through judicial decisions.

Important examples include:

  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Democracy.
  • Republican government.
  • Secularism.
  • Federalism.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Judicial review.
  • Independence of Judiciary.
  • Free and fair elections.
  • The Constitution itself does not contain one exhaustive Article listing every Basic Structure element.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kesavananda Bharati → 1973 → Basic Structure Doctrine

30. Fundamental Rights

  • Fundamental Rights are contained mainly in Part III of the Constitution.
  • Part III covers Articles 12 to 35.
  • Fundamental Rights protect liberty, equality and individual dignity.
  • They impose constitutional limitations on State power.
  • They are generally enforceable through courts.
  • Article 32 provides a constitutional remedy through the Supreme Court.
  • Fundamental Rights form an important feature of India's liberal-democratic constitutional system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Rights → Part III → Articles 12–35

31. Six Categories of Fundamental Rights

The present Fundamental Rights are commonly classified into six groups:

  • Right to Equality.
  • Right to Freedom.
  • Right against Exploitation.
  • Right to Freedom of Religion.
  • Cultural and Educational Rights.
  • Right to Constitutional Remedies.
  • The Right to Property was originally a Fundamental Right.
  • The 44th Constitutional Amendment removed it from the list of Fundamental Rights.
  • Right to Property now exists as a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Right to Property → Not a Fundamental Right

Article 300A → Constitutional Legal Right

32. Directive Principles of State Policy

  • Directive Principles are contained in Part IV.
  • Part IV covers Articles 36 to 51.
  • They provide guidelines to the State for establishing social and economic justice.
  • They promote the concept of a welfare State.
  • They are not directly enforceable by courts.
  • Article 37 declares that they are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPSP → Part IV → Articles 36–51

DPSP → Non-Justiciable

33. Fundamental Duties

  • Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IVA.
  • They are contained in Article 51A.
  • They were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
  • Ten Fundamental Duties were originally added.
  • The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added another duty relating to educational opportunities for children.
  • India therefore presently recognises eleven Fundamental Duties.
  • Fundamental Duties are generally non-justiciable.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Duties → Part IVA → Article 51A

42nd Amendment → Added Duties

Present Duties → 11

34. Rights, Directive Principles and Duties

  • Fundamental Rights protect individual freedom.
  • Directive Principles guide the State towards social and economic welfare.
  • Fundamental Duties emphasise responsibilities of citizens.

Together they reflect the Constitution's attempt to balance:

  • Liberty.
  • Social welfare.
  • Civic responsibility.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Fundamental Rights → Justiciable

DPSP → Non-Justiciable

Fundamental Duties → Generally Non-Justiciable

35. Welfare State Orientation

  • The Constitution seeks to establish more than merely electoral democracy.
  • Directive Principles encourage the State to promote social and economic welfare.
  • The Constitution aims to reduce inequalities.
  • It supports public health, education and livelihood-related welfare objectives.
  • It allows affirmative measures for disadvantaged groups.
  • This gives the Constitution a strong welfare-State orientation.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Constitution → Political Democracy + Social Welfare

36. Secular Constitutional System

  • India has no constitutionally established State religion.
  • The Constitution protects freedom of conscience.
  • Religious freedom is guaranteed subject to constitutional limitations such as public order, morality and health.
  • The State can undertake social reform in constitutionally permissible areas.
  • Secularism has been recognised by the Supreme Court as part of the Basic Structure.
  • The word "Secular" was expressly inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

37. Socialist Orientation

  • The Constitution contains significant commitments to social and economic justice.
  • Directive Principles seek reduction of economic inequalities.
  • Welfare measures and redistributive policies are constitutionally permitted.
  • The word "Socialist" was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
  • Indian constitutional socialism operates within a democratic constitutional framework.

38. Rule of Law

  • Rule of Law means governmental power must operate according to law.
  • Public authorities are subject to constitutional limitations.
  • Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of the laws.
  • Arbitrary governmental action is inconsistent with constitutional governance.
  • Rule of Law has been recognised as part of the Basic Structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 14 → Equality Before Law + Equal Protection of Laws

39. Equality and Social Justice

  • The Constitution protects legal equality.
  • It also permits special constitutional measures for historically disadvantaged groups.
  • Equality does not always require identical treatment in every circumstance.
  • Constitutionally permissible affirmative action seeks substantive equality.
  • Special provisions exist for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, socially and educationally backward classes, women and children.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Equality → Formal Equality + Permissible Affirmative Action

40. Protection of Minorities

  • The Constitution provides safeguards for religious and linguistic minorities.
  • Articles 29 and 30 contain Cultural and Educational Rights.
  • Article 29 protects specified cultural interests.
  • Article 30 gives religious and linguistic minorities constitutional protection regarding establishment and administration of educational institutions.
  • Minority safeguards reflect India's commitment to cultural diversity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Articles 29–30 → Cultural and Educational Rights

41. Abolition of Untouchability and Titles

  • Article 17 abolishes untouchability and prohibits its practice in any form.
  • Article 18 abolishes titles subject to constitutional exceptions for military and academic distinctions.
  • These provisions reflect the republican and egalitarian character of the Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 17 → Abolition of Untouchability

Article 18 → Abolition of Titles

42. Universal Adult Franchise

  • Universal adult franchise was adopted from the beginning of the Republic.
  • Article 326 provides the constitutional basis for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage.
  • The original voting age was 21 years.
  • The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age to 18 years.
  • Adult franchise establishes broad political equality among eligible citizens.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 326 → Adult Suffrage

61st Amendment → Voting Age 21 → 18

43. Single Citizenship

  • India provides single citizenship.
  • A person is constitutionally an Indian citizen rather than holding separate State citizenship.
  • This differs from federal systems such as the United States, where federal and State citizenship coexist.
  • Single citizenship strengthens national unity and common civic identity.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Single Citizenship

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Federalism in India Does Not Mean Separate State Citizenship

44. Common Electoral Citizenship

  • Article 325 provides for one general electoral roll for every territorial constituency.
  • No person can be excluded from an electoral roll merely on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
  • Independent India rejected the colonial system of communal separate electorates.
  • Democratic representation is based on common constitutional citizenship.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Colonial Period → Separate Electorates

Republican Constitution → Common Electoral Framework

45. Independent Election Commission

  • Article 324 provides for the Election Commission of India.

The Election Commission supervises, directs and controls elections to:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures.
  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Independent election administration is a significant safeguard of representative democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 324 → Election Commission of India

46. Bicameral Parliament

Parliament consists constitutionally of:

  • President.
  • Rajya Sabha.
  • Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha is the Council of States.
  • Lok Sabha is the House of the People.
  • The bicameral Parliament enables representation of both the population and the constituent States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 79 → Parliament

Parliament → President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha

47. Rajya Sabha as a Permanent House

  • Rajya Sabha is not subject to dissolution.
  • It is a continuing or permanent House.
  • Approximately one-third of its members retire every second year according to constitutional and statutory arrangements.
  • Lok Sabha, by contrast, is subject to dissolution.
  • This ensures continuity in Parliament.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Rajya Sabha → Permanent House

Lok Sabha → Can Be Dissolved

48. Bicameralism in States

  • Bicameralism is not compulsory for every State.
  • Every State has a Legislative Assembly.
  • Only specified States have a Legislative Council.

A State Legislature may therefore be:

  • Unicameral.
  • Bicameral.
  • Parliament may create or abolish a Legislative Council according to Article 169 after the constitutionally required State Assembly resolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 169 → Creation or Abolition of State Legislative Council

49. Independent Constitutional Bodies

  • The Constitution creates important institutions outside ordinary ministerial departments.

Examples include:

  • Election Commission.
  • Comptroller and Auditor General.
  • Union Public Service Commission.
  • State Public Service Commissions.
  • Finance Commission.
  • These bodies perform specialised constitutional functions and promote institutional accountability.

50. Important Constitutional Body Articles

  • Article 148 → Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
  • Article 280 → Finance Commission.
  • Article 315 → Union and State Public Service Commissions.
  • Article 324 → Election Commission.
  • Article 76 → Attorney-General for India.
📌 Must-Memorise

148 → CAG

280 → Finance Commission

315 → Public Service Commissions

324 → Election Commission

76 → Attorney-General

51. Comptroller and Auditor General

  • The CAG is a constitutional authority.
  • It performs important audit functions concerning public finances.
  • It supports legislative control and accountability over public expenditure.
  • Its constitutional status helps protect institutional independence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 148 → CAG

52. Public Service Commissions

  • The Constitution provides for the Union Public Service Commission.
  • It also provides for State Public Service Commissions.
  • Public Service Commissions advise on constitutionally assigned matters relating to recruitment and public services.
  • Their constitutional status helps promote merit and institutional continuity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 315 → UPSC + State PSCs

53. Finance Commission

  • Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission.
  • It is constituted periodically by the President.
  • It makes recommendations concerning specified financial relations between the Union and States.
  • It is an important institution of fiscal federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 280 → Finance Commission

54. All India Services

  • All India Services are another distinctive feature of Indian administration.
  • Their members are recruited through a national framework but serve under both Union and State governments.

Important examples include:

  • Indian Administrative Service.
  • Indian Police Service.
  • Article 312 provides the constitutional framework for creation of All India Services.
  • They strengthen administrative coordination and national integration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 312 → All India Services

55. Emergency Provisions

  • The Constitution contains provisions for extraordinary situations.
  • National Emergency is provided under Article 352.
  • President's Rule or failure of constitutional machinery in a State is dealt with under Article 356.
  • Financial Emergency is provided under Article 360.
  • Emergency provisions can substantially strengthen Union authority.
  • They therefore constitute an important centralising feature of Indian federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 352 → National Emergency

Article 356 → President's Rule

Article 360 → Financial Emergency

56. Constitution Can Shift towards Greater Centralisation

  • Indian federalism normally operates through constitutionally distributed powers.
  • During specified emergency situations, the Union can obtain expanded authority.
  • This gives the Constitution the ability to respond to extraordinary circumstances.
  • It also explains why Indian federalism is sometimes described as having both federal and unitary features.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Normal Situation → Federal Operation

Emergency Situation → Greater Centralisation Possible

57. Local Self-Government

  • Local government received stronger constitutional recognition through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments.
  • The 73rd Amendment deals with Panchayats.
  • The 74th Amendment deals with Municipalities.
  • These reforms established a constitutional basis for democratic decentralisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

73rd Amendment → Panchayats

74th Amendment → Municipalities

58. Panchayats

  • The 73rd Constitutional Amendment added Part IX.
  • Part IX deals with Panchayats.
  • It also added the Eleventh Schedule.
  • Constitutional provisions deal with Gram Sabha, local elections, reservations and institutional arrangements.
  • Panchayats represent the rural dimension of democratic decentralisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part IX → Panchayats

Eleventh Schedule → Panchayat Subjects

59. Municipalities

  • The 74th Constitutional Amendment added Part IXA.
  • Part IXA deals with Municipalities.
  • It added the Twelfth Schedule.
  • Municipal constitutional provisions strengthen representative urban local government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part IXA → Municipalities

Twelfth Schedule → Municipal Subjects

60. Three-Tier Democratic Structure

  • India was originally constitutionally organised primarily around Union and State governments.
  • The 73rd and 74th Amendments strengthened constitutional recognition of local government.

Indian democratic governance now operates through:

  • Union level.
  • State level.
  • Local level.
  • This expanded grassroots democratic participation.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Democracy → Union + State + Local Levels

61. Reservation in Local Government

  • Constitutional local-government provisions provide reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
  • They also provide reservation for women.
  • At least one-third of specified seats and chairperson positions are constitutionally reserved for women under the basic constitutional scheme.
  • States may provide higher reservation according to law.
  • Local-government reservations expanded political participation among historically underrepresented groups.

62. Fifth Schedule

  • The Fifth Schedule deals with administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
  • It applies to Scheduled Areas outside the special Sixth Schedule framework.
  • It provides special constitutional arrangements for protection and administration of tribal interests.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fifth Schedule → Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes

63. Sixth Schedule

The Sixth Schedule provides special arrangements for specified tribal areas in:

  • Assam.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Tripura.
  • Mizoram.
  • It provides for autonomous institutional arrangements in specified tribal areas.
  • It is distinct from the Fifth Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sixth Schedule → Specified Tribal Areas in Assam + Meghalaya + Tripura + Mizoram

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Fifth Schedule ≠ Sixth Schedule

64. Official Language Framework

  • The Constitution contains detailed provisions concerning language.
  • Article 343 provides that Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union.
  • English continues to be used for Union official purposes under constitutional and statutory arrangements.
  • States may adopt official languages according to constitutional provisions.
  • India's multilingual structure is constitutionally accommodated.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hindi → Official Language of Union

India → No Constitutionally Declared National Language

65. Eighth Schedule

  • The Eighth Schedule contains constitutionally recognised scheduled languages.
  • It originally contained 14 languages.
  • Subsequent constitutional amendments increased the number.
  • It presently contains 22 languages.
  • The Eighth Schedule reflects India's multilingual constitutional character.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eighth Schedule → 22 Scheduled Languages

66. No State Religion

  • The Constitution does not establish an official State religion.
  • Citizens are constitutionally protected in matters of conscience and religion subject to constitutional restrictions.
  • The State is constitutionally required to operate within a secular framework.
  • Religious freedom does not place every activity associated with religion beyond State regulation.

67. Separation of Powers with Checks and Balances

  • India does not follow a completely rigid separation of powers.
  • Legislative, executive and judicial functions are constitutionally distributed.
  • The parliamentary system creates close relations between Legislature and Executive.
  • The Judiciary remains institutionally independent.
  • Constitutional checks prevent any one organ from exercising unlimited authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Functional Separation + Checks and Balances

Not Absolute Separation

68. Social Revolution through Constitutional Methods

  • The Constitution was designed not only to organise institutions but also to transform society.
  • It abolishes untouchability.
  • It protects equality.
  • It allows affirmative-action measures.
  • It protects disadvantaged and minority groups.
  • Directive Principles encourage social and economic welfare.
  • Democratic institutions permit reform through constitutional and legislative methods.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Indian Constitution → Governance + Social Transformation

69. Political Democracy and Social Democracy

  • Elections establish political democracy.
  • Political democracy alone was not considered sufficient by the Constitution-makers.
  • Social democracy requires respect for liberty, equality and fraternity.
  • Ambedkar repeatedly emphasised the relationship between political democracy and social democracy.
  • Constitutional institutions therefore operate alongside social-justice provisions.

70. Constitutional Morality

  • Constitutional government requires more than literal compliance with legal provisions.

Constitutional morality requires respect for:

  • Constitutional procedures.
  • Institutional boundaries.
  • Democratic values.
  • Individual rights.
  • Accountability.
  • Electoral majority alone does not give government unlimited constitutional authority.

71. Living Constitution

  • The Constitution provides institutional stability but also allows adaptation.
  • It changes through formal constitutional amendments.
  • Judicial interpretation develops constitutional meaning.
  • Legislative practices affect constitutional operation.
  • Constitutional conventions influence parliamentary government.
  • Institutional practices evolve over time.
  • The Constitution therefore combines continuity with capacity for change.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Constitution → Stable + Adaptable

72. Salient Features — Federal vs Centralising Features

Federal:

  • Dual government.
  • Written Constitution.
  • Division of powers.
  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Independent Judiciary.
  • Partly rigid amendment procedure.
  • Bicameral Parliament.

Centralising:

  • Strong Union.
  • Union residuary powers.
  • Single citizenship.
  • Integrated Judiciary.
  • Appointed Governors.
  • All India Services.
  • Emergency provisions.
  • Parliament's State-reorganisation power.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

India → Federal Structure + Strong Central Features

73. Salient Features — Rights and Governance

  • Fundamental Rights → Part III.
  • Directive Principles → Part IV.
  • Fundamental Duties → Part IVA.
  • Fundamental Rights → Generally justiciable.
  • Directive Principles → Non-justiciable.
  • Fundamental Duties → Generally non-justiciable.
  • Article 32 → Supreme Court constitutional remedies.
  • Article 226 → High Court writ jurisdiction.
  • Article 14 → Equality.
  • Article 17 → Untouchability abolished.
  • Article 18 → Titles abolished.

74. Salient Features — Democratic Institutions

  • Parliamentary government.
  • Representative democracy.
  • Universal adult franchise.
  • Independent Election Commission.
  • Bicameral Parliament.
  • Collective ministerial responsibility.
  • Periodic elections.
  • Single citizenship.
  • Constitutional local self-government.

75. Salient Features — Important Articles

  • Article 1 → Union of States.
  • Article 13 → Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
  • Article 14 → Equality before law.
  • Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability.
  • Article 18 → Abolition of titles.
  • Article 32 → Constitutional remedies.
  • Article 51A → Fundamental Duties.
  • Article 75(3) → Collective responsibility of Union Council of Ministers.
  • Article 79 → Parliament.
  • Article 148 → CAG.
  • Article 280 → Finance Commission.
  • Article 312 → All India Services.
  • Article 315 → Public Service Commissions.
  • Article 324 → Election Commission.
  • Article 326 → Adult suffrage.
  • Article 343 → Official language of Union.
  • Article 352 → National Emergency.
  • Article 356 → President's Rule.
  • Article 360 → Financial Emergency.
  • Article 368 → Constitutional amendment.

76. Salient Features — Important Parts

  • Part III → Fundamental Rights.
  • Part IV → Directive Principles of State Policy.
  • Part IVA → Fundamental Duties.
  • Part IX → Panchayats.
  • Part IXA → Municipalities.

77. Salient Features — Important Schedules

  • Fifth Schedule → Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
  • Sixth Schedule → Specified tribal areas in Northeast.
  • Seventh Schedule → Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
  • Eighth Schedule → Scheduled Languages.
  • Tenth Schedule → Anti-Defection.
  • Eleventh Schedule → Panchayat subjects.
  • Twelfth Schedule → Municipal subjects.

78. TNPSC Traps

  • India → Parliamentary, not presidential government.
  • President → Constitutional head.
  • Prime Minister → Real political executive.
  • Council of Ministers → Collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
  • India → Federal structure with strong Centre.
  • Article 1 → Union of States.
  • K.C. Wheare → Quasi-federal.
  • "Quasi-federal" → Not constitutional wording.
  • Residuary powers → Parliament.
  • Constitution → Supreme over Parliament.
  • Indian Constitution → Partly rigid + partly flexible.
  • Judiciary → Independent and integrated.
  • Judicial review → Constitutional safeguard.
  • Kesavananda Bharati → 1973 → Basic Structure.
  • Fundamental Rights → Part III.
  • DPSP → Part IV.
  • Fundamental Duties → Part IVA.
  • Fundamental Rights → Generally justiciable.
  • DPSP → Non-justiciable.
  • Fundamental Duties → Generally non-justiciable.
  • Right to Property → Not a Fundamental Right.
  • Article 300A → Right to Property.
  • Article 326 → Adult suffrage.
  • Voting age → 18.
  • 61st Amendment → Voting age reduced from 21 to 18.
  • India → Single citizenship.
  • Article 324 → Election Commission.
  • Parliament → President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha → Permanent House.
  • Every State does not have a Legislative Council.
  • Article 169 → Creation/abolition of State Legislative Council.
  • Article 352 → National Emergency.

  • Article 360 → Financial Emergency.
  • 73rd Amendment → Panchayats.

  • Part IXA → Municipalities.
  • Fifth Schedule ≠ Sixth Schedule.
  • Hindi → Official language of Union.
  • India → No constitutionally declared national language.
  • Eighth Schedule → 22 languages.
  • India → No State religion.
  • Separation of powers → Not absolute.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

Is the Indian Constitution written or unwritten? → Written.

Why is it considered detailed? → It contains extensive provisions dealing with institutions, federalism, rights, administration and constitutional procedures.

How many Articles did the original Constitution contain? → 395.

How many Parts? → 22.

How many Schedules? → 8.

Did India simply copy foreign constitutions? → No. Foreign provisions were selectively adapted to Indian conditions.

Which country influenced parliamentary government? → United Kingdom.

Which country influenced Fundamental Rights and judicial review? → United States.

Which country influenced DPSP? → Ireland.

Which country influenced strong-Centre federalism? → Canada.

Which country influenced Concurrent List and joint sitting? → Australia.

Which country influenced Fundamental Duties? → Former Soviet Union.

Which country influenced emergency provisions? → Weimar Germany.

Which country influenced constitutional amendment procedure? → South Africa.

Which country influenced "procedure established by law"? → Japan.

What form of government does India follow? → Parliamentary government.

Who is the constitutional head of the Union? → President.

Who is the real political executive? → Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

To which House is the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible? → Lok Sabha.

Which Article provides collective responsibility? → Article 75(3).

Does India follow a federal system? → Yes, with strong centralising features.

What are the main federal features? → Dual government, division of powers, written Constitution, constitutional supremacy, independent Judiciary, partial rigidity and bicameralism.

What are important centralising features? → Strong Union, residuary powers, single citizenship, integrated Judiciary, appointed Governors, All India Services, emergencies and State-reorganisation power.

Which Article describes India as a Union of States? → Article 1.

Who described India as quasi-federal? → K.C. Wheare.

Is "quasi-federal" written in the Constitution? → No.

Which Schedule distributes legislative subjects? → Seventh Schedule.

What are the three lists? → Union List, State List and Concurrent List.

Who possesses residuary legislative powers? → Parliament.

Can States constitutionally secede from the Union? → No.

Can Parliament alter State boundaries? → Yes, according to constitutional procedure.

Is the Constitution rigid or flexible? → It combines both rigidity and flexibility.

Which Article deals with constitutional amendment? → Article 368.

What is supreme in India? → Constitution.

Does India follow unlimited parliamentary sovereignty? → No.

What type of Judiciary does India have? → Independent and integrated Judiciary.

What is the judicial hierarchy? → Supreme Court → High Courts → Subordinate Courts.

What is judicial review? → Judicial examination of legislative and executive action for constitutional validity.

Which Article relates laws to Fundamental Rights? → Article 13.

Which Article allows approaching the Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights enforcement? → Article 32.

Which Article gives High Courts writ jurisdiction? → Article 226.

Which case established the Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973.

Can Parliament amend the Constitution? → Yes.

Can it destroy the Basic Structure? → No.

Which Part contains Fundamental Rights? → Part III.

Which Articles broadly contain Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12–35.

How many categories of Fundamental Rights presently exist? → Six.

Is Right to Property a Fundamental Right? → No.

Which Article protects Right to Property? → Article 300A.

Which Part contains DPSP? → Part IV.

Which Articles broadly contain DPSP? → Articles 36–51.

Are DPSP enforceable by courts? → No.

Which Article declares DPSP fundamental in governance? → Article 37.

Which Part contains Fundamental Duties? → Part IVA.

Which Article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A.

Which Amendment introduced Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976.

How many Duties were originally added? → Ten.

How many are there now? → Eleven.

Which Amendment added the eleventh Fundamental Duty? → 86th Amendment, 2002.

Does India have a State religion? → No.

Is secularism part of the Basic Structure? → Yes.

Which Article guarantees equality before law? → Article 14.

Which Article abolishes untouchability? → Article 17.

Which Article abolishes titles? → Article 18.

Which Articles deal with cultural and educational rights? → Articles 29 and 30.

What is universal adult franchise? → Voting right for eligible adult citizens subject to constitutional and legal qualifications.

Which Article provides adult suffrage? → Article 326.

What was the original voting age? → 21.

What is the present voting age? → 18.

Which Amendment reduced it? → 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988.

Does India provide single or dual citizenship? → Single citizenship.

Which Article provides one general electoral roll? → Article 325.

Did independent India continue communal separate electorates? → No.

Which Article provides for the Election Commission? → Article 324.

What constitutes Parliament? → President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.

Which Article defines Parliament? → Article 79.

Which House of Parliament is permanent? → Rajya Sabha.

Can Rajya Sabha be dissolved? → No.

Does every State have a Legislative Council? → No.

Which Article deals with creation or abolition of a Legislative Council? → Article 169.

Which Article provides for CAG? → Article 148.

Which Article provides for Finance Commission? → Article 280.

Which Article provides for Public Service Commissions? → Article 315.

Which Article provides for All India Services? → Article 312.

What is the National Emergency Article? → Article 352.

Which Article deals with President's Rule? → Article 356.

Which Article deals with Financial Emergency? → Article 360.

Which Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayats? → 73rd Amendment.

Which Part deals with Panchayats? → Part IX.

Which Schedule deals with Panchayat subjects? → Eleventh Schedule.

Which Amendment gave constitutional status to Municipalities? → 74th Amendment.

Which Part deals with Municipalities? → Part IXA.

Which Schedule deals with Municipal subjects? → Twelfth Schedule.

Which Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes? → Fifth Schedule.

Which Schedule deals with special tribal arrangements in specified northeastern States? → Sixth Schedule.

Which States are specifically associated with the Sixth Schedule? → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

Which Article states the official language of the Union? → Article 343.

What is the official language of the Union under Article 343? → Hindi in Devanagari script.

Is Hindi constitutionally India's national language? → No.

How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22.

Does India follow absolute separation of powers? → No.

What does India follow? → Functional separation with checks and balances.
